Problem: evaluating calibration and selective prediction of a System-1 model on biosecurity-relevant benchmarks; assessing reliability.

Method: audit of commercial System-1 model measuring accuracy, calibration, error detection, selective prediction; also answer-order study; use of confidence field and max probability; compute expected calibration error, AUROC, selective prediction curves (accuracy vs coverage).

Key assumptions: not explicitly stated; maybe that the vendor's uncertainty field can be interpreted as calibrated; we can note assumption that the confidence field is an affine rescaling of p_max.

Main contribution: reliability audit showing moderate calibration (ECE 0.034) and AUROC 0.820; discovery of answer-order instability causing 37.4% of items to change answer under option permutations; averaging probabilities across rotations improves accuracy.

Datasets: 6,020 multiple-choice items from WMDP, WMDP-Bio variant, six LAB-Bench subtasks.

Benchmarks: WMDP, WMDP-Bio, WMDP-Cyber, LAB-Bench subtasks (maybe not standard). Not exactly language/vision benchmarks but related to biological reasoning.

Baselines: maybe not; they compare different uncertainty fields (vendor field vs pmax).

Metrics: accuracy, expected calibration error (ECE), AUROC, selective prediction (accuracy vs coverage), answer-order stability.

Results: model reasonably well calibrated (pooled ECE 0.034); top-1 probability separates correct from incorrect predictions (pooled AUROC 0.820); under four cyclic rotations, 37.4% of WMDP-Cyber items receive different answers; averaging probabilities across rotations improves WMDP-Cyber accuracy by +3.8 points; applying averaging only to low-confidence items recovers most gain at low cost.

Limitations: calibration quality varies across datasets; small item counts for some subsets lead to higher ECE; answer-order instability suggests sensitivity to trivial perturbations.

Future work: not explicitly stated; maybe extend to other System-1 models, investigate causes of answer-order instability, develop methods to mitigate.

Now we have abstract. We'll analyze this paper.

Problem: automated skin-lesion classifiers have high aggregate performance but lack reliability for individual predictions; need to know when to trust a prediction.

Method: reframe as reliability-aware selective prediction; train transparent tree-ensemble classifiers with reliability layer combining max class confidence, predictive entropy, post-hoc temperature scaling, and confidence/entropy-based accept-defer rules; evaluate on HAM10000 and ISIC 2018 datasets.

Key assumptions: not explicit; maybe that combining confidence, entropy, and temperature scaling yields reliable uncertainty estimates.

Main contribution: reliability-aware selective prediction framework with temperature scaling calibration, confidence/entropy-based deferral, class-aware referral (malignancy-aware) reducing miss rate.

Datasets: HAM10000 (10,015 images) and ISIC 2018 (Malignant vs Benign) (3,297 images).

Benchmarks: not explicitly; they compare raw performance vs reliability layer.

Baselines: raw classifier (without reliability layer), maybe global confidence deferral.

Metrics: accuracy, balanced accuracy, AUROC for error detection, expected calibration error (ECE), accepted-case accuracy, error routing rate, melanoma miss rate.

Results: temperature scaling reduces ECE from 0.120 to 0.028 (76.5% reduction) on HAM10000; accepting most reliable half raises accepted-case accuracy to 0.905 while routing 83.7% of errors to expert review; malignancy-aware referral reduces melanoma miss rate from 26.9% to 7.6% at matched coverage and below 1% at higher deferral. Similar results on ISIC 2018.

Limitations: not stated; maybe limited to dermatology datasets; reliability layer may add overhead.

Future work: not stated.

Code availability: not stated.

Overlap with idea: problem overlap medium (both concern reliability via calibration and selective prediction), method overlap medium (both use post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling) and threshold-based accept/defer rules), evaluation overlap low (different domain: medical imaging vs language/vision).
